A Tax With Cliffs

HAWAIʻI TAXES EVERY SALE OF REAL PROPERTY when the deed is recorded. The rate depends on the price and applies to the whole of it, so the tax jumps at each threshold: a home that sells for $3,999,000 pays 0.5 percent, or $19,995, and one that sells for $4,000,000 pays 0.7 percent, or $28,000. Buyers who cannot claim a county homeowner exemption, because the home will not be their main residence, pay a slightly higher schedule (Table 1).1

The tax raised $96 million in fiscal year 2025.2 The first 10 percent, up to $5.1 million, goes to the land conservation fund and half, up to $38 million, to the rental housing revolving fund. The rest goes to the general fund.3

Today’s rate applies to the whole price of a sale in the band. The draft’s rate applies only to the part of the price within the band, and the total is capped at 4 percent of the price for owner-occupants and 6 percent for other buyers. Today’s owner-occupant schedule also covers commercial, agricultural and other nonresidential property, and the draft keeps it for them.

What SB 3028 Would Change

THE LAST DRAFT OF SB 3028 would tax home sales the way the income tax taxes income: each rate applies only to the part of the price within its band.4 For a buyer who will live in the home, the part of the price between $2 million and $3 million would be taxed at 2 percent and the part between $3 million and $6 million at 4 percent. For other buyers, those rates would be 5 percent and 7 percent. The band edges would rise each year with consumer prices, starting in 2027. Nonresidential property would stay on today’s schedule.

Because the rates below $2 million would change little and apply only to each slice of the price, the draft cuts the tax on most home sales up to $2,247,000 for owner-occupants and $2,073,000 for other buyers. The exceptions are sales just under $2 million, from $1,801,000 and $1,681,000, where today’s rate is still 0.3 or 0.4 percent of the price; they would pay up to $300 or $800 more. Above $2,247,000 and $2,073,000 the draft raises the tax, steeply (Table 2). House Finance Committee Chair Chris Todd gave the same thresholds, about $2.3 million and $2.1 million, when his committee approved the draft in April 2026.5

House and Senate negotiators met through May 1 without agreeing, and the bill died with the session.6 The draft is the fullest statement of where the Legislature left the idea, and the model scores its rates as written, as if enacted in 2027.

Who Would Pay More

MOST SALES WOULD PAY THE SAME OR LESS. Maui is the one county that publishes every sale with its price and the conveyance tax paid.7 Of its sales in recent years, 43 percent would pay less under the draft and 42 percent the same, mostly because they are nonresidential or sell for less than $600,000. The other 15 percent would pay more. Chair Todd put the statewide share paying the same or less at 91 percent, and this estimate gives 90 percent of home sales statewide; Maui’s is lower because it has more expensive homes than the rest of the state, relative to its size (Table 4).

Nearly all of the new revenue would come from the top of the market. On Maui, sales above $4 million would provide 88 percent of it, and buyers who will not make the home their main residence 92 percent. Statewide the share is about the same, 88 percent. Even on Oʻahu, where most homes worth $2 million or more are lived in by their owners, those homes sell less often than second homes and rentals, and their buyers pay the lower owner-occupant rates.

The $3 Million to $4 Million Home

A HOME SELLING FOR $3.5 MILLION to a family that will live in it pays $17,500 in conveyance tax today. Under the draft it would pay $46,300. Sold to anyone else, it would pay $93,800 instead of $21,000. This is where the draft turns steep: at $3 million the rate on each added dollar jumps to 4 percent for owner-occupants and 7 percent for other buyers, while today’s rate holds at 0.5 or 0.6 percent of the price up to $4 million.

At fiscal year 2028 prices, about 69 Maui homes a year sell for $3 million to $4 million, 50 of them to buyers who will not live in them. Those buyers’ average tax would rise from $20,510 to $83,624. For owner-occupants it would rise from $16,855 to $38,511. Even so, the band provides only 10 percent of Maui’s new revenue, because far more money changes hands above it (Figure 1).

The draft also ends today’s cliff at $4 million. Under it, a sale at $3,999,000 and one at $4,000,000 would owe almost the same, $66,260 and $66,300 for an owner-occupant, where today they differ by $8,005. These are the amounts due at the sale; part of a tax on sales can be passed back to sellers through the price.

What It Would Raise

STATEWIDE, THE DRAFT WOULD RAISE an estimated $79 million more than current law in fiscal year 2028, the first full year a bill passed in 2027 could reach. That is on top of about $120 million the tax would raise anyway. Before accounting for fewer sales, the increase would be $119 million.8

Transfer taxes discourage sales. The estimates assume sales fall 6 percent for each point of the price the draft adds in tax, and rise where it cuts the tax. That is the figure the United Kingdom’s Office for Budget Responsibility uses for homes over £1 million, based on the UK’s 2014 switch from cliff rates to rates on slices of the price, the same change the draft would make,9 and about what Los Angeles’s tax on sales over $5 million did to sales of single-family homes.10 Hawaiʻi’s tax falls on the deed, so a home owned by a company can change hands untaxed if the buyer buys the company instead, and nothing about such a sale has to be reported.1112 On Oʻahu, companies own 62 percent of the homes worth $10 million or more that their owners do not live in.13 The estimates assume that a quarter of sales at $4 million or more by companies, to buyers who will not live in the home, would go that way. A sales response of 4 to 10 percent per point, with none to half of those company sales escaping, gives $56 million to $98 million.

Maui County would provide $23 million and Oʻahu $24 million, though Maui has only 17 percent of the state’s home sales by value in this estimate to Oʻahu’s 56 percent. The difference is who owns the expensive homes. Of Maui’s 6,461 homes worth $2 million or more, 66 percent are not lived in by their owners; of Oʻahu’s 14,786, 38 percent. Second homes and rentals sell more often and pay the higher rates (Figure 3 and Table 4).

The increase grows each year, though a little more slowly than home prices. As prices rise, more of each sale falls in the higher bands, but indexing the bands to consumer prices offsets part of that, and the fall in sales deepens as the added tax grows. The model assumes home prices rise 4 percent a year and consumer prices 3 percent. By fiscal year 2031 the increase reaches $86 million (Figure 4).

Checking against the House. Chair Todd said the draft would raise about $20 million a year less than the roughly $170 million of the House’s original proposal, HB 2049 HD3, which puts it near $150 million.518 The House’s method is not public, but two of its figures can be checked. Scored the same way, before any change in sales, HB 2049 HD3 would raise $21 million more than the draft in fiscal year 2028, and 90 percent of home sales would pay the same or less under the draft (78 percent under HB 2049, against Rep. Evslin’s 75 percent). The House’s levels are higher: its $150 million is 1.3 times this estimate before any change in sales in fiscal year 2028, and 1.6 times at 2023 to 2026 prices ($94 million). The Department of Taxation’s estimate for a 2025 bill with the introduced SB 3028’s rates, HB 1410 HD2, which also put commercial sales on a sliding scale, is 1.4 times what this model gives for it.19

Where the Money Would Go

THE DRAFT ALSO REWRITES who gets the money. Before any reaches the general fund, it would send 5 percent, up to $10 million, to the land conservation fund; 20 percent, up to $40 million, to the rental housing revolving fund; 30 percent, up to $60 million, to the Hawaiian home lands infrastructure and housing special fund; and 20 percent, up to $40 million, to transit-oriented development infrastructure.4

Those shares add up to 75 percent of all conveyance tax, including the tax on sales the draft leaves unchanged, until the funds reach their caps. The general fund therefore comes out ahead only if the draft raises more than about $107 million a year, more than this estimate. In fiscal year 2028 the general fund would receive $50 million, $27 million less than under current law, while the four funds together would receive $149 million. Even at the top of the range, the general fund would receive $9 million less (Table 7).

How These Estimates Are Made

BECAUSE TODAY’S TWO SCHEDULES DIFFER, the tax recorded on a Maui sale shows which one applied, and so whether the buyer could claim a homeowner exemption. Of sales with a price and tax in fiscal years 2023 to 2026, 98 percent match one schedule to within half a percent; the rest are treated as nonresidential, whose tax the draft leaves alone. The county’s land-use codes separate owner-occupied homes from nonresidential property on the owner-occupant schedule, and land with no home on it, which the draft keeps on today’s schedule, from homes. A deed that covers several parcels counts once. Applied to the sorted home sales, current law reproduces the tax Maui recorded on them to within a few hundred dollars a year. The model uses about 2,640 sales a year in all.7

No other county publishes a file of its sales with prices (their property search sites show sales a parcel at a time, under terms that bar collecting them in bulk), so the other three are built from their own records with Maui’s as the template. Joining every Maui sale to the county’s assessment listing shows how often homes of each assessed value sell, split by whether their owners live in them, which kind of buyer bought them, and at what price relative to the assessment. Oʻahu, Hawaiʻi Island and Kauaʻi publish the same kind of records home by home: the City’s assessment tables, which list every parcel and condominium unit with its value and exemptions;14 Hawaiʻi County’s parcel records, whose condominium projects are split into units and whose homeowners’ values, which the county caps, are restored to market;15 and Kauaʻi County’s property tax records, which give each parcel’s market value.16 Applying Maui’s rates to those homes gives each county’s sales by price, spread around each home’s assessed value as prices are on Maui.

From $1 million up, those sales are then matched, price band by price band, to each county’s own sales: its house and condominium sales in the multiple listing service, times the ratio of all recorded home sales to listed ones on Maui, where both are known, with an allowance on Oʻahu for condominium towers whose first sales are not listed.17 That brings in, in Maui’s proportions, the sales Maui’s rates leave out, such as vacant lots and transfers at nominal prices. On Hawaiʻi Island, the match calls for 1.4 to 1.9 times as many sales from $1 million to $10 million as Maui’s rates give its homes. Applied to Maui’s own homes, the same steps recover 97 percent of Maui’s increase, and the other counties are scaled by the difference. Buildings of five or more units are left out of the rates and the counts, as are records worth $20 million or more that are not condominium units or known single homes, since most are apartment or resort properties.

Three checks. Oʻahu’s owner records, compared between December 2023 and September 2026, show its homes assessed at $4 million or more changing hands 1.6 times as often as Maui’s rates imply,20 but its listed sales show about as many sales at those prices as Maui’s rates give (1.05 times): its most expensive homes appear to sell for less, relative to their assessments, than Maui’s. Using Oʻahu’s turnover with Maui’s prices instead would add $9 million (Table 8). Second, today’s tax on the modeled home sales in the three counties comes to $48 million a year at 2023 to 2026 prices, leaving 36 percent of their collections to commercial and other property, against 24 percent on Maui.2 If the share were the same, the modeled home sales would be about 19 percent short. Third, the House’s and the Department of Taxation’s figures run above this estimate (above). All three suggest the estimate is more likely low than high. Sales of apartment buildings with five or more units are scored under the draft’s rule that sets the rate by the price per unit, which lowers their tax; on Maui there were 17 such sales in four years. Left out: long-term leases; the draft’s rule taxing former vacation rentals at the higher rates whoever buys them; Maui homes on agricultural or other nonresidential land, which the draft would newly treat as residential (on Hawaiʻi Island and Kauaʻi they are counted as homes); and any effect on prices. The sales behind the estimate, from 2023 to 2026, came in a slow market: the tax raised about $95 million a year then, against $188 million in fiscal year 2022. In a stronger market both the tax and the increase would be larger. The full method and every parameter are in the source code.8

This page was revised three times in September 2026. The first version scaled Maui’s results up by the conveyance tax each county group paid and gave $69 million to $118 million after fewer sales; the first revision, scaling by each county’s value above $2 million on its tax roll, gave $67 million; the second, building Oʻahu and Hawaiʻi Island from their homes at Maui’s sale rates, gave $70 million. This version matches each county to its own sales by price, builds Kauaʻi from its parcel values, counts once the Maui deeds that cover several parcels, which the second version counted once per parcel, overstating the estimate by about 4 percent, and takes the response of sales from the evidence of the UK and Los Angeles.

  • disposition.csv: revenue by fund, fiscal year 2028
  • summary.json: shares of sales paying more and less, the $3 million to $4 million figures, and the checks above
